html:
Samuel de Champlain was a French explorer and mapmaker who founded Quebec in 1608 and built New France into a lasting colony. He is often called the father of New France.

Born in the port of Brouage in western France around 1574, he first sailed up the St. Lawrence in 1603. That year at Tadoussac he joined an alliance between the French and the Innu, who wanted French help and goods against the Haudenosaunee. From 1604 to 1607 he helped found a French post in Acadia and mapped the coast south to Cape Cod, where his men clashed with the Nauset.

His alliances shaped everything that followed:

  • In 1609 he went south with Algonquin, Wendat and Innu warriors and shot dead Mohawk chiefs at the lake that now bears his name. This bound the French to their allies and made the Haudenosaunee their enemies for decades.
  • In 1615 he travelled up the Ottawa River to the country of the Wendat, the heart of the fur trade.

Quebec stayed tiny. English privateers captured it in 1629, and it was returned to France in 1632. Champlain came back as its leader and died there on Christmas Day 1635. His maps and books were the best accounts of the region for years.
